chapters.title: 17. A Restless Day
paragraphs: On Friday morning, that is, the day after the accursed performance, the entire available staff of the Variety—the accountant Vasily Stepanovich Lastochkin, two bookkeepers, three typists, both cashiers, the messengers, the ushers and the cleaning women—in short, everyone who was on hand, was not at their posts doing their work but was sitting on the sills of the windows that looked out on Sadovaya, watching what was going on beneath the Variety’s wall. Beneath that wall, in a double row, clung a queue many thousands strong, whose tail reached all the way to Kudrinskaya Square. At the head of this queue stood some two dozen ticket touts well known in theatrical Moscow.

The queue was in a state of great excitement, drew the attention of the citizens streaming past, and was busy discussing the inflammatory stories about the previous day’s unheard-of performance of black magic. These same stories threw the accountant Vasily Stepanovich, who had not been at the show the night before, into the greatest confusion. The ushers were telling God knows what, including how, after the famous performance ended, certain female citizens had run about the street in an indecent state, and other things of the same sort. Modest, quiet Vasily Stepanovich only blinked as he listened to the tall tales about all these wonders, and had absolutely no idea what to do, and yet something had to be done, and it had to be done by him, since he now turned out to be the senior man in the whole Variety team.

By ten in the morning the queue of people craving tickets had swollen so much that rumors of it reached the police, and with astonishing speed both foot and mounted patrols were sent, which did bring the queue into some sort of order. Yet even an orderly snake a kilometer long was in itself a great temptation and left the citizens on Sadovaya utterly amazed.

That was outside, but inside the Variety things were not right either. From very early in the morning the telephones began to ring, and rang without stopping, in Likhodeyev’s office, in Rimsky’s office, in the accounts department, in the box office and in Varenukha’s office. At first Vasily Stepanovich gave some sort of answer, the cashier answered too, the ushers mumbled something into the phone, but then they stopped answering altogether, because to the questions of where Likhodeyev, Varenukha and Rimsky were there was absolutely nothing to say. At first they tried to get off with the words “Likhodeyev is at his apartment,” but callers from town replied that they had called the apartment and the apartment said that Likhodeyev was at the Variety.

An agitated lady called and began demanding Rimsky; she was advised to call his wife, to which the receiver, bursting into sobs, replied that she was his wife and that Rimsky was nowhere to be found. Some sort of nonsense was beginning. The cleaning woman had already told everybody that when she came into the financial director’s office to clean, she found the door wide open, the lamps burning, the window onto the garden smashed, the armchair lying on the floor and nobody there.

Some time after ten Madame Rimskaya burst into the Variety. She was sobbing and wringing her hands. Vasily Stepanovich was completely at a loss and did not know what to advise her. And at half past ten the police arrived. Their very first and perfectly reasonable question was:
“What’s going on here, citizens? What’s the matter?”

The team stepped back, pushing the pale and agitated Vasily Stepanovich to the front. There was nothing for it but to call things by their names and admit that the Variety’s administration, in the persons of the director, the financial director and the house manager, had vanished and was who knew where, that the master of ceremonies had been taken to a psychiatric hospital after the previous day’s performance, and that, to put it briefly, this performance of the day before had been nothing short of a scandal.

Madame Rimskaya, still sobbing, was calmed as far as possible and sent home, and the greatest interest was shown in the cleaning woman’s story of the state in which the financial director’s office had been found. The staff were asked to go to their places and get on with their work, and a short while later the investigation appeared in the Variety building, accompanied by a sharp-eared, muscular dog the color of cigarette ash, with extraordinarily intelligent eyes. A whisper at once spread among the Variety staff that the dog was none other than the famous Tuzbuben. And so it was. His behavior astonished everyone. The moment Tuzbuben ran into the financial director’s office, he growled, baring monstrous yellowish fangs, then lay down on his belly and, with a kind of anguish and at the same time fury in his eyes, crawled toward the broken window. Overcoming his fear, he suddenly leaped onto the windowsill, raised his sharp muzzle upward and howled wildly and savagely. He would not leave the window, growled and shuddered and kept trying to jump down.

The dog was led out of the office and let loose in the lobby; from there he went out through the main entrance onto the street and led those following him to the taxi rank. There he lost the trail he had been following. After that Tuzbuben was driven away.

The investigation settled in Varenukha’s office and began calling in, one by one, those members of the Variety staff who had witnessed the previous day’s incidents during the performance. It must be said that at every step the investigation had to overcome unforeseen difficulties. The thread kept snapping in its hands.

There were posters, weren’t there? There were. But overnight they had been pasted over with new ones, and now there was not a single one left, not for the life of them! Where had this magician of theirs come from? Well, who knows. So there must have been a contract with him?
“One would assume so,” the agitated Vasily Stepanovich replied.
“And if there was a contract, then it must have gone through the accounts department?”
“Without fail,” Vasily Stepanovich replied, growing agitated.
“Then where is it?”

“It isn’t there,” replied the accountant, turning paler and paler and spreading his hands. And indeed, neither in the files of the accounts department, nor in the financial director’s office, nor in Likhodeyev’s or Varenukha’s, was there any trace of a contract.

What was the magician’s name, then? Vasily Stepanovich does not know, he was not at the performance yesterday. The ushers do not know; the ticket cashier wrinkled her forehead and wrinkled it, thought and thought, and finally said:
“Wo... Woland, I think.”
But maybe it wasn’t Woland? Maybe it wasn’t Woland. Maybe it was Faland.
It turned out that the foreigners’ bureau had heard absolutely nothing of any Woland, or for that matter of any Faland, a magician.

The messenger Karpov reported that this same magician had supposedly been staying at Likhodeyev’s apartment. The apartment, of course, was visited at once. No magician was found there. Likhodeyev himself was not there either. The housekeeper Grunya was not there, and where she had got to nobody knew. The chairman of the tenants’ association, Nikanor Ivanovich, was not there, Prolezhnev was not there!

What emerged was something utterly preposterous: the entire top of the administration had vanished, yesterday there had been a strange, scandalous performance, and who had put it on, and at whose instigation, was unknown.

Meanwhile it was getting on toward noon, when the box office was due to open. But that, of course, was out of the question! An enormous piece of cardboard was hung on the doors of the Variety at once, reading: “Today’s performance is canceled.” Unrest broke out in the queue, beginning at its head, but after some unrest it began all the same to break up, and an hour or so later not a trace of it remained on Sadovaya. The investigation departed to continue its work elsewhere, the staff were sent home, only those on duty being kept, and the doors of the Variety were locked.

The accountant Vasily Stepanovich urgently had two tasks to carry out. First, to go to the Commission for Spectacles and Entertainments of the Lighter Kind with a report on the previous day’s incidents, and second, to call at the Spectacles Finance Sector in order to hand in the previous day’s takings—21,711 roubles.

Neat and dutiful, Vasily Stepanovich wrapped the money in newspaper, tied the package crosswise with string, put it in his briefcase and, knowing his instructions perfectly well, set off, naturally, not for a bus or a tram, but for the taxi rank.

The moment the drivers of three cars saw a passenger hurrying to the rank with a tightly stuffed briefcase, all three drove off empty from under his nose, for some reason glancing back at him spitefully as they did so.
Struck by this circumstance, the accountant stood rooted to the spot for a long time, trying to work out what it could mean.
About three minutes later an empty car rolled up, and the driver’s face twisted the moment he saw the passenger.
“Is the car free?” asked Vasily Stepanovich, coughing in surprise.
“Show me your money,” the driver answered spitefully, without looking at the passenger.
More and more astonished, the accountant, clamping the precious briefcase under his arm, pulled a ten-rouble note out of his wallet and showed it to the driver.
“I’m not going!” the man said curtly.
“I beg your pardon...” the accountant began, but the driver cut him off:
“Got any threes?”
Completely bewildered, the accountant took two three-rouble notes out of his wallet and showed them to the driver.
“Get in,” the man shouted, and slapped down the flag of the meter so hard that he nearly broke it. They drove off.
“No change, is that it?” the accountant asked timidly.

“A pocketful of change!” the driver bawled, and his eyes, filling with blood, were reflected in the little mirror. “Third time it’s happened to me today. And the same thing’s happened to the others. Some son of a bitch hands me a ten, I give him change—four-fifty... Out he gets, the swine! Five minutes later I look: instead of a ten, the label off a Narzan bottle!” Here the driver uttered several unprintable words. “Another one—past Zubovskaya. A ten. I give him three roubles change. Off he goes! I reach into my purse, and out of it a bee—snap, right on the finger! Ah, you!..” The driver again stuck in some unprintable words. “And no ten. Yesterday at that Variety” (unprintable words) “some viper of a conjuror put on a show with ten-rouble notes” (unprintable words)...
The accountant went numb, shrank into himself and put on the air of someone hearing the very word “Variety” for the first time, while he thought: “Well, well!..”

Arriving where he needed to go and paying without mishap, the accountant entered the building and hurried down the corridor toward the office of the head, and on the way he already understood that he had come at a bad time. Some sort of commotion reigned in the offices of the Spectacles Commission. A messenger woman ran past the accountant, her kerchief slipping to the back of her head and her eyes popping.
“He’s not there, he’s not there, he’s not there, my dears!” she was shouting, addressing no one knew whom. “The jacket and trousers are here, but there’s nothing in the jacket!”

She vanished behind some door, and at once the sound of breaking dishes was heard behind it. The head of the commission’s first sector, whom the accountant knew, ran out of the secretary’s room, but he was in such a state that he did not recognize the accountant, and vanished without a trace.
Shaken by all this, the accountant made his way to the secretary’s room, which served as the anteroom to the office of the chairman of the commission, and here he was utterly astounded.

From behind the closed door of the office came a menacing voice, undoubtedly belonging to Prokhor Petrovich, the chairman of the commission. “Giving someone a dressing-down, is he?” thought the bewildered accountant, and, looking around, he saw something else: in a leather armchair, her head thrown back against it, sobbing uncontrollably, a wet handkerchief in her hand, her legs stretched out almost to the middle of the secretary’s room, lay Prokhor Petrovich’s personal secretary, the beautiful Anna Richardovna.
Anna Richardovna’s whole chin was smeared with lipstick, and black streams of running mascara were creeping from her lashes down her peach-like cheeks.
Seeing that someone had come in, Anna Richardovna jumped up, rushed at the accountant, seized the lapels of his jacket and began shaking him and shouting:

“Thank God! At least one brave man has turned up! They’ve all run away, they’ve all betrayed him! Come, come to him, I don’t know what to do!” And, still sobbing, she dragged the accountant into the office.
Once inside the office, the accountant first of all dropped his briefcase, and every thought in his head turned upside down. And, it must be said, with good reason.

At the enormous desk with its massive inkstand sat an empty suit, moving a dry pen, not dipped in ink, across a sheet of paper. The suit had a tie on, a fountain pen stuck out of the suit’s breast pocket, but above the collar there was neither neck nor head, just as no hands peeped out of the cuffs. The suit was absorbed in its work and took absolutely no notice of the turmoil reigning all around. Hearing that someone had come in, the suit leaned back in its chair, and above the collar rang out the voice of Prokhor Petrovich, well known to the accountant:
“What is it? It says on the door, doesn’t it, that I’m not receiving anyone.”
The beautiful secretary gave a shriek and, wringing her hands, cried out:
“You see? You see?! He’s not there! He’s not there! Bring him back, bring him back!”

At that moment someone poked his head in at the office door, gasped and flew out again. The accountant felt his legs begin to tremble and sat down on the edge of a chair, but did not forget to pick up his briefcase. Anna Richardovna jumped around the accountant, tugging at his jacket, and kept crying out:

“I always, always stopped him when he swore by the devil! And now he’s sworn himself to the devil!” Here the beauty ran up to the desk and cried in a sweet, musical voice, a little nasal after her crying: “Prosha! Where are you?”
“Who’s ‘Prosha’ to you here?” the suit inquired haughtily, sinking still deeper into its chair.
“He doesn’t recognize me! He doesn’t recognize me! Do you understand?” the secretary sobbed.

“I’ll ask you not to sob in my office!” said the hot-tempered striped suit, now getting angry, and with its sleeve it drew toward itself a fresh pile of papers, with the evident aim of writing resolutions on them.
“No, I can’t watch this, no, I can’t!” Anna Richardovna screamed and ran out into the secretary’s room, and after her the accountant shot out like a bullet.

“Imagine, I’m sitting here,” Anna Richardovna was telling him, shaking with agitation and clutching the accountant’s sleeve again, “and in comes a cat. Black, huge, like a behemoth. Of course I shout ‘Shoo!’ at it. Out it goes, and in its place in comes a fat man, also with a sort of cat’s mug, and says: ‘Now what’s this, citizen, shouting “shoo” at visitors?’ And straight in he slips to Prokhor Petrovich. Of course I go after him, shouting: ‘Are you out of your mind?’ And he, the brazen thing, goes straight to Prokhor Petrovich and sits down in the armchair facing him! Well, he... he’s the kindest soul there is, but nervous. He flared up! I don’t deny it. A nervous man, works like an ox—he flared up. ‘What do you mean,’ he says, ‘barging in without being announced?’ And that impudent creature, just imagine, sprawls in the armchair and says, smiling: ‘Why, I’ve come,’ he says, ‘to talk over a little matter with you.’ Prokhor Petrovich flared up again: ‘I’m busy!’ And the other one, just think of it, answers: ‘You’re not busy with anything at all...’ Eh? Well, that, of course, was when Prokhor Petrovich’s patience snapped, and he cried out: ‘What is all this? Get him out of here, devils take me!’ And the other one, imagine, smiled and says: ‘Devils take you? Why not, that can be done!’ And—crash—before I could cry out, I look: the one with the cat’s mug isn’t there, and there s... sits... the suit... Eeeee!..” Anna Richardovna howled, stretching her mouth, which had lost all shape entirely.
Choking on a sob, she caught her breath, but then poured out something quite incoherent:
“And he writes and writes and writes! It’s enough to drive you mad! He talks on the telephone! A suit! They’ve all scattered like hares!”

The accountant only stood there and trembled. But here fate came to his rescue. Into the secretary’s room, with a calm, businesslike step, came the police, two of them. Seeing them, the beauty sobbed still harder, jabbing her hand toward the door of the office.

“Let’s not sob, citizen,” the first one said calmly, and the accountant, feeling that he was quite superfluous here, slipped out of the secretary’s room and a minute later was already in the fresh air. There was a sort of draft in his head, a hum as in a chimney, and in this hum could be heard scraps of the ushers’ stories about yesterday’s cat, which had taken part in the performance. “Aha-ha! Could that be our pussycat, by any chance?”

Having got nowhere at the commission, the conscientious Vasily Stepanovich decided to call at its branch, which was housed in Vagankovsky Lane. And, to calm himself a little, he made the journey to the branch on foot.
The City Spectacles Branch was housed in a mansion, peeling with age, at the back of a courtyard, and was famous for the porphyry columns in its lobby.
But it was not the columns that astonished the branch’s visitors that day; it was what was going on beneath them.

Several visitors stood frozen, staring at a weeping young lady sitting at a little table on which lay the specialist literature on spectacles that the young lady sold. At that moment the young lady was not offering anyone any of this literature and only waved away sympathetic questions, while from above and below and from the sides, from every department of the branch, there poured the ringing of at least twenty telephones, all straining themselves hoarse.
After weeping a while, the young lady suddenly gave a start and shrieked hysterically:
“There it goes again!” And unexpectedly she began to sing in a trembling soprano:
Glorious sea, sacred Baikal...
A messenger who had appeared on the stairs shook his fist at someone and began to sing along with the young lady in a toneless, dull baritone:
Glorious ship, an omul barrel!..

Distant voices joined the messenger’s voice, the choir began to swell, and at last the song thundered in every corner of the branch. In the nearest room, No. 6, which housed the audit and accounts department, someone’s powerful, slightly husky basso profundo stood out in particular. The choir was accompanied by the swelling clatter of the telephones.
Hey, Barguzin... stir up the swell!..—bawled the messenger on the stairs.
Tears flowed down the girl’s face; she tried to clench her teeth, but her mouth opened of its own accord, and she sang an octave higher than the messenger:
The brave lad has not far to go!

What astonished the speechless visitors to the branch was that the singers, scattered in different places, sang very harmoniously, as though the whole choir were standing with its eyes fixed on an invisible conductor.
Passers-by in Vagankovsky Lane stopped at the courtyard railings, marveling at the merriment reigning in the branch.
As soon as the first verse came to an end, the singing suddenly stopped, again as if at the conductor’s baton. The messenger swore softly and disappeared.
Here the front doors opened, and in them appeared a citizen in a summer coat from under which the skirts of a white coat stuck out, and with him a policeman.
“Do something, doctor, I beg you!” the girl cried hysterically.
The secretary of the branch ran out onto the stairs and, evidently burning with shame and embarrassment, began, stammering:
“You see, doctor, we have a case of some sort of mass hypnosis... So, it is necessary...” He did not finish the sentence, began to choke on his words, and suddenly started singing in a tenor:
Shilka and Nerchinsk...
“Idiot!” the girl managed to shout, but did not explain whom she was abusing, and instead produced a forced roulade and herself began to sing about Shilka and Nerchinsk.
“Pull yourself together! Stop singing!” the doctor said to the secretary.

By every sign the secretary would himself have given anything to stop singing, but stop he could not, and together with the choir he carried to the ears of the passers-by in the lane the news that in the wilds the ravenous beast had not touched him and the hunters’ bullet had not caught him!
The moment the verse ended, the girl was the first to receive a dose of valerian from the doctor, and then he ran after the secretary to the others, to dose them too.
“Excuse me, miss,” Vasily Stepanovich suddenly addressed the girl, “a black cat hasn’t dropped in on you, has it?..”
“Cat? What cat?” the girl shouted in a fury. “It’s an ass we’ve got sitting in this branch, an ass!” And, adding to that: “Let him hear! I’ll tell everything,” she did indeed tell what had happened.
It turned out that the head of the city branch, who had “made a complete mess of light entertainment” (in the girl’s words), suffered from a mania for organizing clubs of every kind.
“Pulling the wool over his bosses’ eyes!” the girl yelled.

In the course of a year the head had managed to organize a club for the study of Lermontov, a chess and draughts club, a ping-pong club and a horse-riding club. By summer he was threatening to organize a freshwater rowing club and a mountaineering club.
And so today, during the lunch break, in he comes, the head...

“And leading some son of a bitch by the arm,” the girl was saying, “who’d come from no one knows where, in measly little checked trousers, in a cracked pince-nez, and... a mug that was simply impossible!”
And right then and there, according to the girl’s story, he introduced him to everyone eating in the branch’s canteen as a prominent specialist in organizing choral clubs.

The faces of the future mountaineers darkened, but the head at once called on everyone to cheer up, and the specialist cracked jokes, made witticisms and swore up and down that singing took up only the tiniest bit of time, while the benefit of this singing, by the way, was a whole wagonload.

Well, naturally, as the girl reported, the first to jump forward were Fanov and Kosarchuk, the branch’s most notorious toadies, who announced that they were signing up. At this the rest of the staff realized there was no escaping the singing, and they had to sign up for the club as well. They decided to sing during the lunch break, since all the rest of the time was taken up with Lermontov and draughts. To set an example, the head announced that he was a tenor, and from then on everything went as in a bad dream. The checked specialist and choirmaster bellowed:

“Do-mi-sol-do!” He dragged the shyest out from behind the cupboards where they had tried to escape the singing, told Kosarchuk that he had perfect pitch, whined, whimpered, begged them to humor an old choirmaster and songbird, rapped his tuning fork on his fingers, imploring them to strike up “Glorious Sea.”

They struck up. And they struck up gloriously. The checked man really did know his business. They sang the first verse to the end. Here the choirmaster excused himself, said, “Back in a minute!” and... vanished. They thought he really would come back in a minute. But ten minutes went by, and he was not there. Joy seized the branch workers: he had run off.

And suddenly, somehow of their own accord, they began to sing the second verse. Kosarchuk led them all, who perhaps did not have perfect pitch but did have a rather pleasant high tenor. They sang it through. No choirmaster! They went back to their places, but before they could sit down they began to sing against their will. Stop? Not a chance. They would be silent for three minutes or so and then strike up again. Silence—then they strike up! Here they realized that something was badly wrong. The head locked himself in his office for shame.
At this point the girl’s story broke off. The valerian had been no help at all.
A quarter of an hour later three lorries drove up to the railings in Vagankovsky Lane, and the entire staff of the branch, with the head in the lead, was loaded onto them.

The moment the first lorry, swaying in the gateway, drove out into the lane, the staff, standing on the platform and holding one another by the shoulders, opened their mouths, and the whole lane rang with the popular song. The second lorry took it up, and the third after it. And so they drove off. Passers-by hurrying about their business cast only a fleeting glance at the lorries, not the least surprised, assuming it was an excursion heading out of town. They were indeed heading out of town, only not on an excursion, but to Professor Stravinsky’s clinic.

Half an hour later the accountant, who had completely lost his head, reached the Spectacles Finance Sector, hoping at last to be rid of the state’s money. Taught by experience now, he first of all cautiously peered into the long hall where the employees sat behind frosted glass with gold lettering. Here the accountant found no sign of alarm or outrage. It was quiet, as is proper in a respectable institution.
Vasily Stepanovich put his head through the little window over which was written “Receipt of Sums,” greeted some employee he did not know, and politely asked for a receipt slip.
“And what do you want it for?” asked the employee at the window.
The accountant was astonished.
“I want to hand in a sum. I’m from the Variety.”
“One moment,” the employee replied, and instantly covered the hole in the glass with a grille.

“Strange!” thought the accountant. His astonishment was perfectly natural. For the first time in his life he had come up against such a circumstance. Everyone knows how hard it is to get money; there can always be obstacles to that. But in the accountant’s thirty years of practice there had never been a case of anyone, be it a legal entity or a private person, having difficulty accepting money.
But at last the little grille slid aside, and the accountant again pressed himself to the window.
“And is it a lot?” asked the employee.
“Twenty-one thousand seven hundred and eleven roubles.”
“Oho!” the employee replied, for some reason ironically, and held out a green form to the accountant.
Knowing the form well, the accountant filled it in in a flash and began untying the string on the package. When he had unwrapped his load, his eyes swam, and he gave a sort of pained moan.
Before his eyes flashed foreign money. There were bundles of Canadian dollars, English pounds, Dutch guilders, Latvian lats, Estonian kroons...
“There he is, one of those tricksters from the Variety,” came a menacing voice above the dumbstruck accountant. And at once Vasily Stepanovich was arrested.

chapters.title: 18. Luckless Visitors
paragraphs: At the very time when the diligent accountant was speeding along in a taxi to run into the self-writing suit, there stepped out, among other passengers, from reserved soft-class carriage No. 9 of the Kiev train that had just arrived in Moscow, a respectable passenger with a small fiberboard suitcase in his hand. This passenger was none other than the uncle of the late Berlioz, Maximilian Andreyevich Poplavsky, an economic planner, residing in Kiev on what used to be Institutskaya Street. The reason for Maximilian Andreyevich’s coming to Moscow was a telegram he had received late in the evening two days before, which read as follows:
“I have just been run over by tram at Patriarch’s.
Funeral Friday, three in afternoon. Come. Berlioz.”

Maximilian Andreyevich was considered, and deservedly so, one of the cleverest men in Kiev. But even the cleverest man can be stumped by a telegram like this. If a man telegraphs that he has been run over, it is clear that he has not been run over fatally. But then what has the funeral to do with it? Or is he in a very bad way and foresees that he will die? That is possible, but this precision is strange in the highest degree—how on earth does he know for certain that he will be buried on Friday at three in the afternoon? An astonishing telegram!

However, clever people are clever precisely so that they can sort out muddled things. It was very simple. A mistake had been made, and the dispatch had been transmitted garbled. The words “I have” had undoubtedly strayed in here from another telegram, in place of the words “Berlioz has,” which had turned into plain “Berlioz” and wandered to the end of the telegram. With this correction the meaning of the telegram became clear, though, of course, tragic.
When the outburst of grief that struck Maximilian Andreyevich’s wife had subsided, he at once began getting ready for Moscow.

It behooves us to reveal one of Maximilian Andreyevich’s secrets. There is no denying that he was sorry for his wife’s nephew, who had perished in the prime of life. But, as a practical man, he naturally understood that there was no particular need for his presence at the funeral. And nevertheless Maximilian Andreyevich was in a great hurry to get to Moscow. What was the matter? Just one thing—the apartment. An apartment in Moscow! That is serious. For no known reason Maximilian Andreyevich did not like Kiev, and the thought of moving to Moscow had been gnawing at him so much lately that he had even begun to sleep badly.

He took no joy in the spring floods of the Dnieper, when the water, flooding the islands by the low bank, merged with the horizon. He took no joy in the view, staggering in its beauty, that opened out from the foot of the monument to Prince Vladimir. He was not cheered by the patches of sunlight playing in spring on the brick paths of Vladimir Hill. He wanted none of this, he wanted just one thing—to move to Moscow.

Advertisements in the newspapers offering to exchange an apartment on Institutskaya Street in Kiev for smaller quarters in Moscow produced no result. No takers turned up, and if on rare occasions some did, their offers were dishonest.
The telegram shook Maximilian Andreyevich. This was a moment it would be a sin to let slip. Practical people know that such moments do not come twice.

In short, whatever the difficulties, he had to manage to inherit his nephew’s apartment on Sadovaya. Yes, it was complicated, very complicated, but these complications had to be overcome at all costs. The experienced Maximilian Andreyevich knew that the first and indispensable step to this end had to be the following: he had to get himself registered, if only temporarily, as a resident of his late nephew’s three rooms.
On Friday afternoon Maximilian Andreyevich walked through the door of the room that housed the management office of building No. 302-bis on Sadovaya Street in Moscow.

In the narrow little room, where an old poster hung on the wall showing in several pictures the methods of reviving people drowned in a river, there sat at a wooden table, all alone, an unshaven, middle-aged man with anxious eyes.
“May I see the chairman of the tenants’ association?” the economic planner politely inquired, taking off his hat and setting his little suitcase on an empty chair.
This seemingly simple little question for some reason upset the seated man, so that his face even changed. Squinting anxiously, he muttered indistinctly that the chairman was not there.
“Is he at home in his apartment?” asked Poplavsky. “I have a most urgent matter.”
The seated man again answered very incoherently. But all the same it could be guessed that the chairman was not at home either.
“And when will he be in?”
The seated man made no reply to this and looked out of the window with a sort of anguish.
“Aha!” the clever Poplavsky said to himself, and inquired about the secretary.

The strange man at the table even turned purple with the strain and said, again indistinctly, that the secretary was not there either... when he would come was not known and... that the secretary was ill...
“Aha!..” Poplavsky said to himself. “But surely there’s someone on the association board?”
“Me,” the man responded in a weak voice.

“You see,” Poplavsky began impressively, “I am the sole heir of the late Berlioz, my nephew, who perished, as you know, at Patriarch’s, and I am obliged by law to take possession of the inheritance, which consists of our apartment number fifty...”
“I’m not up on this, comrade...” the man interrupted wretchedly.
“But excuse me,” said Poplavsky in a ringing voice, “you are a member of the board and are obliged...”
And here some citizen came into the room. At the sight of the newcomer the man sitting at the table turned pale.
“Board member Pyatnazhko?” the newcomer asked the seated man.
“Yes,” the man answered barely audibly.
The newcomer whispered something to the seated man, and he, thoroughly upset, rose from his chair, and a few seconds later Poplavsky was left alone in the empty board room.
“Ah, what a complication! And why did they all have to be at once...” Poplavsky thought in vexation, crossing the asphalt courtyard and hurrying to apartment No. 50.

The moment the economic planner rang, the door was opened, and Maximilian Andreyevich went into the dim front hall. He was somewhat surprised by the circumstance that it was not clear who had opened the door for him: there was nobody in the front hall except an enormous black cat sitting on a chair.

Maximilian Andreyevich coughed and stamped his feet, and then the door of the study opened, and Koroviev came out into the front hall. Maximilian Andreyevich bowed to him politely but with dignity, and said:
“My name is Poplavsky. I am the uncle...”
But before he could finish, Koroviev snatched a dirty handkerchief from his pocket, buried his nose in it and began to weep.
“...of the late Berlioz...”

“Of course, of course,” Koroviev interrupted, taking the handkerchief from his face. “The moment I glanced at you I guessed it was you!” Here he began to shake with tears and to cry out: “What a calamity, eh? What on earth is going on? Eh?”
“Run over by a tram?” Poplavsky asked in a whisper.

“Clean through!” Koroviev cried, and tears poured from under his pince-nez in streams. “Clean through! I was a witness. Would you believe it—bang! Head—off! Right leg—crunch, in half! Left leg—crunch, in half! That’s what these trams lead to!” And, evidently unable to control himself, Koroviev pecked his nose against the wall beside the mirror and began to shake with sobs.

Berlioz’s uncle was sincerely struck by the stranger’s behavior. “And they say there are no warm-hearted people in our day!” he thought, feeling that his own eyes were beginning to itch. Yet at the same time an unpleasant little cloud passed over his soul, and at once the thought flickered like a little snake: what if this warm-hearted man had already got himself registered in the late man’s apartment? For such things too had happened in life.

“Forgive me, were you a friend of my late Misha?” he asked, wiping his dry left eye with his sleeve and studying the grief-shaken Koroviev with his right. But the man was sobbing so hard that nothing could be made out except the repeated words “crunch—and in half!” Having sobbed his fill, Koroviev at last unstuck himself from the wall and brought out:
“No, I can’t bear any more! I’ll go and take three hundred drops of valerian in ether!..” And, turning his thoroughly tear-stained face to Poplavsky, he added: “That’s trams for you!”
“Excuse me, was it you who sent me the telegram?” asked Maximilian Andreyevich, racking his brains as to who this astonishing crybaby could be.
“He did!” Koroviev replied, and pointed his finger at the cat.
Poplavsky goggled, thinking he had misheard.

“No, I haven’t the strength, I can’t bear it,” Koroviev went on, sniffling, “when I remember: the wheel over the leg... a single wheel weighs a good ten poods... Crunch!.. I’ll go and lie down in bed and sink into oblivion,” and at that he vanished from the front hall.
The cat, however, stirred, jumped down from the chair, stood up on its hind legs, put its paws on its hips, opened its maw and said:
“Well, I sent the telegram. What of it?”
Maximilian Andreyevich’s head at once began to spin, his arms and legs went numb, he dropped his suitcase and sat down on a chair facing the cat.
“I believe I’m asking you in plain Russian,” the cat said sternly. “What of it?”
But Poplavsky gave no answer whatever.
“Passport!” the cat yapped, and held out a plump paw.

Understanding nothing and seeing nothing except the two sparks burning in the cat’s eyes, Poplavsky snatched his passport from his pocket like a dagger. The cat took a pair of spectacles in thick black frames from the table under the mirror, put them on its muzzle, which made it even more impressive, and took the passport out of Poplavsky’s twitching hand.
“Now I wonder: will I faint or won’t I?” thought Poplavsky. From far off came Koroviev’s sobbing; the whole front hall filled with the smell of ether, valerian and some other nauseating abomination.
“What office issued this document?” asked the cat, peering at the page. No answer followed.

“The four hundred and twelfth,” the cat said to itself, running its paw over the passport, which it was holding upside down. “Why, of course! I know that office! They’ll issue a passport to anybody there! Whereas I, for instance, would never have issued one to the likes of you! Never in a million years! I’d have taken just one look at your face and refused on the spot!” The cat got so angry that it flung the passport on the floor. “Your attendance at the funeral is canceled,” the cat went on in an official voice. “Kindly return to your place of residence.” And it barked through the door: “Azazello!”

At its call there ran out into the front hall a small, limping man, sheathed in black tights, with a knife stuck in his leather belt, red-haired, with a yellow fang and a white film over his left eye.
Poplavsky felt that he was short of air, got up from the chair and backed away, clutching his heart.
“Azazello, see him out!” the cat ordered, and left the front hall.
“Poplavsky,” the newcomer twanged quietly through his nose, “I hope everything is clear by now?”
Poplavsky nodded.
“Go back to Kiev at once,” Azazello went on, “sit there quieter than water and lower than grass, and don’t dream of any apartments in Moscow, understood?”

This little man, who reduced Poplavsky to mortal terror with his fang, his knife and his crooked eye, came up only to the economist’s shoulder, but he acted energetically, smoothly and in an organized fashion.

First of all he picked up the passport and handed it to Maximilian Andreyevich, who took the little book with a dead hand. Then the one called Azazello picked up the suitcase with one hand, flung the door open with the other and, taking Berlioz’s uncle by the arm, led him out onto the landing. Poplavsky leaned against the wall. Without any key Azazello opened the suitcase, took out of it an enormous roast chicken minus one leg, wrapped in a grease-soaked newspaper, and laid it on the landing. Then he pulled out two changes of underwear, a razor strop, some book and a case, and kicked all of it, except the chicken, down the stairwell. The emptied suitcase flew after it. It could be heard crashing down below and, judging by the sound, its lid flew off.

Then the red-haired brigand seized the chicken by its leg and with the whole of this chicken, flat, struck Poplavsky on the neck so hard and so terribly that the body of the chicken bounced off and the leg remained in Azazello’s hands. Everything was in confusion in the Oblonskys’ house, as the famous writer Leo Tolstoy so rightly put it. That is exactly what he would have said in this case. Yes! Everything was in confusion in Poplavsky’s eyes. A long spark shot past his eyes, then gave way to a sort of funereal snake that blotted out the May day for an instant—and Poplavsky went flying down the stairs, his passport in his hand. Reaching the turn, he kicked out the windowpane on the next landing and sat down on a step. The legless chicken hopped past him and tumbled down the stairwell. Azazello, who had stayed upstairs, gnawed the chicken leg clean in an instant, stuck the bone in the side pocket of his tights, went back into the apartment and shut himself in with a crash.
At that moment the cautious footsteps of someone coming up began to be heard from below.
Running down one more flight, Poplavsky sat down on a small wooden bench on the landing and caught his breath.
A tiny elderly man with an extraordinarily sad face, in an old-fashioned tussore-silk suit and a hard straw hat with a green band, coming up the stairs, stopped beside Poplavsky.
“Allow me to ask you, citizen,” the little man in tussore inquired sadly, “where is apartment number fifty?”
“Further up!” Poplavsky answered curtly.
“I thank you most humbly, citizen,” the little man said just as sadly, and went on up, while Poplavsky got up and ran down.

The question arises: was Maximilian Andreyevich perhaps hurrying to the police to complain about the brigands who had committed savage violence upon him in broad daylight? No, by no means, that can be said with confidence. To walk into the police and say that, look here, just now a cat in spectacles was reading my passport, and then a man in tights, with a knife... no, citizens, Maximilian Andreyevich was truly a clever man!

He was already downstairs and saw, right next to the street door, a door leading into some little cubbyhole. The glass in this door had been knocked out. Poplavsky put his passport away in his pocket and looked around, hoping to see his thrown-out belongings. But there was no trace of them. Poplavsky himself marveled at how little this upset him. He was occupied by another interesting and tempting thought: to test the accursed apartment once more on this little man. Indeed: since he had asked where it was, he must be going there for the first time. So he was now heading straight into the clutches of that gang that had dug itself into apartment No. 50. Something told Poplavsky that the little man would very soon come out of that apartment. Maximilian Andreyevich, of course, no longer had any intention of going to any funeral of any nephew, and there was plenty of time before the Kiev train. The economist looked around and dived into the cubbyhole.

At that moment a door banged far above. “That’s him going in...” Poplavsky thought with a sinking heart. It was cool in the cubbyhole, and it smelled of mice and boots. Maximilian Andreyevich settled on some wooden stump and decided to wait. The position was a convenient one: from the cubbyhole there was a direct view of the street door of the sixth entrance.

However, he had to wait longer than the Kievan had expected. For some reason the stairs remained deserted the whole time. Sounds carried well, and at last a door banged on the fifth floor. Poplavsky froze. Yes, those were his little steps. “He’s coming down.” A door opened one floor lower. The little steps stopped. A woman’s voice. The voice of the sad little man... yes, it was his voice... Said something like “leave me be, for Christ’s sake...” Poplavsky’s ear was sticking out through the broken glass. This ear caught a woman’s laughter. Quick, brisk steps coming down; and then the back of a woman flashed by. This woman, with a green oilcloth bag in her hands, went out of the entrance into the courtyard. And the little man’s little steps started up again. “Strange! He’s going back up to the apartment! Could he be one of that gang himself? Yes, he’s going back. There, they’ve opened the door upstairs again. Well then, we’ll wait some more.”
This time he did not have to wait long. Sounds of the door. Little steps. The little steps stopped. A desperate cry. The mewing of a cat. Little steps, quick, pattering, down, down, down!

Poplavsky’s wait was rewarded. Crossing himself and muttering something, the sad little man flew past, hatless, with a completely deranged face, a scratched bald head and thoroughly wet trousers. He began tugging at the handle of the street door, so frightened that he could not work out which way it opened, outward or inward; at last he got the better of it and flew out into the sunlit courtyard.

The test of the apartment had been carried out. Thinking no more of either his late nephew or the apartment, shuddering at the thought of the danger he had been exposed to, Maximilian Andreyevich, whispering only two words, “It’s all clear! It’s all clear!”, ran out into the courtyard. A few minutes later a trolleybus was carrying the economic planner off in the direction of the Kiev Station.

As for the little man, while the economist was sitting in the cubbyhole downstairs, a most unpleasant thing had happened to him. The little man was the barman at the Variety, and his name was Andrei Fokich Sokov. While the investigation was going on at the Variety, Andrei Fokich had kept himself apart from everything that was happening, and only one thing had been noticed: that he had grown even sadder than he always was in general, and, besides that, that he had asked the messenger Karpov where the visiting magician was staying.
And so, having parted from the economist on the landing, the barman made his way up to the fifth floor and rang at apartment No. 50.

The door was opened at once, but the barman gave a start, backed away and did not go in straightaway. This was understandable. The door had been opened by a girl who had nothing on except a coquettish little lace apron and a white headpiece. On her feet, it is true, were little golden slippers. The girl’s figure was flawless, and the only defect in her appearance might be considered a livid scar on her neck.
“Well, come in, since you rang!” said the girl, fixing her green, wanton eyes on the barman.

Andrei Fokich gasped, blinked and stepped into the front hall, taking off his hat. Just at that moment the telephone rang in the front hall. The shameless maid, putting one foot up on a chair, took the receiver off the hook and said into it:
“Hello!”

The barman did not know where to put his eyes, shifted from one foot to the other and thought: “Some maid the foreigner has! Ugh, what filth!” And, to save himself from the filth, he began glancing sideways around the room.

The whole large, dim front hall was cluttered with unusual objects and garments. Thus, a mourning cloak lined with fire-colored cloth had been thrown over the back of a chair, and on the table under the mirror lay a long sword with a gleaming gold hilt. Three swords with silver hilts stood in the corner as simply as any umbrellas or walking sticks. And on a stag’s antlers hung berets with eagle feathers.

“Yes,” the maid was saying into the phone. “What? Baron Meigel? I’m listening. Yes! The artiste is at home today. Yes, he will be glad to see you. Yes, guests... Tailcoat or black jacket. What? By midnight.” Having finished the conversation, the maid put down the receiver and turned to the barman: “What can I do for you?”
“I must see the citizen artiste.”
“What? Actually him, himself?”
“Him,” the barman replied sadly.
“I’ll ask,” said the maid, evidently hesitating, and, opening the door to the late Berlioz’s study a little, announced: “Knight, there’s a little man here who says he needs Messire.”
“Why, let him come in,” came Koroviev’s cracked voice from the study.
“Go through to the drawing room,” said the girl, as simply as if she were dressed like a human being; she opened the door to the drawing room a little and herself left the front hall.

On entering where he had been invited, the barman even forgot about his business, so struck was he by the furnishings of the room. Through the colored panes of the big windows (a fancy of the jeweler’s widow, who had vanished without a trace) poured an extraordinary light, like the light in a church. In the enormous old fireplace, despite the hot spring day, logs were blazing. And yet it was not in the least hot in the room; quite the opposite, a sort of cellar dampness seized whoever came in. In front of the fireplace, on a tiger skin, sat a huge black tomcat, blinking good-naturedly at the fire. There was a table at the sight of which the God-fearing barman gave a start: the table was covered with church brocade. On the brocade cloth stood a multitude of bottles—pot-bellied, moldy and dusty. Among the bottles gleamed a dish, and one could see at once that the dish was of pure gold. At the fireplace a small red-haired man with a knife in his belt was roasting pieces of meat on a long steel sword, and the juice dripped into the fire, and the smoke went off up the flue. There was a smell not only of roasting, but also of some very strong perfume and of incense, which made the barman, who already knew from the newspapers of Berlioz’s death and of where he had lived, wonder fleetingly whether, heaven forbid, they had held a church requiem for Berlioz—a thought, however, which he at once drove away as obviously absurd.
The stunned barman unexpectedly heard a heavy bass voice:
“Well, sir, how can I be of use to you?”
Only then did the barman discover in the shadows the one he needed.

The black magician was sprawled on some boundless sofa, a low one, with cushions scattered on it. As it seemed to the barman, the artiste had on only black underwear and black, pointy-toed slippers to match.
“I,” the barman began bitterly, “am the manager of the buffet at the Variety Theatre...”
The artiste stretched out his hand, on whose fingers gems flashed, as though to stop the barman’s mouth, and spoke with great heat:

“No, no, no! Not another word! Not on any account, and never! I won’t put a thing in my mouth from your buffet! My most esteemed sir, I walked past your counter yesterday, and to this day I cannot forget either the sturgeon or the brynza. My precious fellow! Brynza is never green, someone has deceived you. It is supposed to be white. Yes, and the tea? Why, it’s slops! With my own eyes I saw some slovenly girl topping up your enormous samovar from a bucket of unboiled water, while they went on pouring out the tea all the same. No, my dear fellow, this is impossible!”
“I beg your pardon,” began Andrei Fokich, stunned by this sudden attack, “I’m not here about that, and the sturgeon has nothing to do with it.”
“What do you mean, nothing to do with it, when it’s gone off!”
“The sturgeon was delivered second-grade fresh,” the barman informed him.
“My dear fellow, that is nonsense!”
“What is nonsense?”
“Second-grade freshness—that is what is nonsense! There is only one freshness—the first, and it is also the last. And if sturgeon is second-grade fresh, that means it is rotten!”
“I beg your pardon...” the barman began again, not knowing how to get rid of the artiste who was picking on him.
“I cannot pardon you,” the man said firmly.
“I didn’t come about that,” the barman said, now thoroughly upset.

“Not about that?” the foreign magician was surprised. “Then what other business could have brought you to me? If my memory does not fail me, of persons close to you in profession I have been acquainted with only one sutler woman, and that was long ago, before you were born. However, I am glad. Azazello! A stool for the buffet manager!”
The one who was roasting the meat turned around, horrifying the barman with his fangs as he did so, and deftly handed him one of the low, dark oak stools. There were no other seats in the room.
The barman uttered:

“I thank you most humbly,” and lowered himself onto the little stool. Its back leg at once broke with a crack, and the barman, with a gasp, struck his backside most painfully on the floor. As he fell, he caught with his foot another little stool standing in front of him, and from it upset a full goblet of red wine onto his trousers.
The artiste exclaimed:
“Ai! Haven’t you hurt yourself?”

Azazello helped the barman up and gave him another seat. In a voice full of woe the barman declined his host’s suggestion that he take off his trousers and dry them in front of the fire and, feeling unbearably uncomfortable in his wet underwear and clothes, sat down warily on the other stool.

“I like to sit low,” the artiste went on. “It’s not so dangerous to fall from low down. Yes, so, we stopped at the sturgeon? My dear fellow! Freshness, freshness and freshness—that is what should be the motto of every barman. But here, would you care to taste...”

Here, in the crimson light from the fireplace, a sword flashed before the barman, and Azazello laid a sizzling piece of meat on a golden plate, poured lemon juice over it and handed the barman a golden two-pronged fork.
“Most humbly... I...”
“No, no, do try it!”

Out of politeness the barman put a little piece in his mouth and at once realized that he was chewing something really very fresh and, above all, extraordinarily tasty. But as he chewed the fragrant, juicy meat, the barman nearly choked and fell a second time. Out of the next room flew a big dark bird, which brushed the barman’s bald head lightly with its wing. When it settled on the mantelpiece next to the clock, the bird turned out to be an owl. “Lord God almighty!” thought Andrei Fokich, who was nervous, like all barmen. “What an apartment!”
“A goblet of wine? White, red? What country’s wine do you prefer at this time of day?”
“Most humbly... I don’t drink...”
“A pity! Then perhaps you would like a game of dice? Or do you prefer some other games? Dominoes, cards?”
“I don’t play,” replied the barman, already worn out.

“Very bad indeed,” the host concluded. “Say what you like, there is something not good lurking in men who avoid wine, games, the company of charming women and table talk. Such people are either gravely ill or secretly hate those around them. True, exceptions are possible. Among the persons who have sat down with me at the banqueting table there have sometimes been astonishing scoundrels! And so, I am listening to your business.”
“Yesterday you were pleased to do some conjuring tricks...”
“I?” exclaimed the magician in astonishment. “Have mercy. It is somehow not even becoming to me!”
“Sorry,” said the taken-aback barman, “but... the performance of black magic...”

“Ah, yes, yes, of course! My dear fellow! I will tell you a secret: I am not an artiste at all, I simply wanted to see the Muscovites en masse, and the most convenient place to do that was in a theater. And so my retinue,” he nodded toward the cat, “arranged this performance, while I merely sat and looked at the Muscovites. But don’t change countenance; tell me, what has brought you to me in connection with this performance?”

“If you please, among other things, some bits of paper came floating down from the ceiling...” The barman lowered his voice and glanced around in embarrassment. “Well, everybody grabbed them. And then a young man comes into my buffet, gives me a ten-rouble note, I give him eight and a half roubles change... Then another...”
“Also a young man?”

“No, an elderly one. A third, a fourth... I keep giving change. And today I started checking the till, I look, and instead of money there’s cut-up paper. They did the buffet out of a hundred and nine roubles.”
“Ai-yai-yai!” exclaimed the artiste. “Did they really think those were real notes? I cannot admit the thought that they did it knowingly.”
The barman glanced around somehow crookedly and miserably, but said nothing.
“Can they be swindlers?” the magician anxiously asked his guest. “Can there be swindlers among the Muscovites?”
In reply the barman smiled so bitterly that all doubts fell away: yes, there are swindlers among the Muscovites.
“That is low!” Woland was indignant. “You are a poor man... You are a poor man, aren’t you?”
The barman drew his head into his shoulders, so that it became evident that he was a poor man.
“How much have you got in savings?”
The question was asked in a sympathetic tone, but all the same such a question cannot be considered other than indelicate. The barman faltered.
“Two hundred and forty-nine thousand roubles in five savings banks,” a cracked voice responded from the next room, “and at home under the floor two hundred gold ten-rouble pieces.”
The barman seemed to have become welded to his stool.
“Well, of course, that is no sum at all,” Woland said condescendingly to his guest, “though, as a matter of fact, you have no need of it either. When are you going to die?”
At this the barman became indignant.
“That is known to nobody and is nobody’s concern,” he replied.

“Oh yes, not known,” came the same wretched voice from the study. “As if it were Newton’s binomial theorem! He’ll die in nine months, in February of next year, of liver cancer, in the clinic of First Moscow State University, in ward four.”
The barman’s face turned yellow.

“Nine months,” Woland calculated pensively. “Two hundred and forty-nine thousand... That comes to twenty-seven thousand a month in round figures? Not a lot, but enough for a modest life... And then there are those gold pieces...”

“There’ll be no cashing in the gold pieces,” the same voice joined in, freezing the barman’s heart. “On Andrei Fokich’s death the house will be pulled down at once, and the gold pieces will be sent to the State Bank.”

“And I would not advise you to go into the clinic,” the artiste went on. “What sense is there in dying in a ward to the groans and wheezing of hopeless patients? Would it not be better to throw a feast with these twenty-seven thousand and, having taken poison, pass over to the sound of strings, surrounded by tipsy beauties and dashing friends?”
The barman sat motionless and had grown much older. Dark rings surrounded his eyes, his cheeks sagged, and his lower jaw dropped.
“However, we are daydreaming,” the host exclaimed. “To business. Show me your cut-up paper.”
The barman, agitated, pulled a bundle out of his pocket, unwrapped it and was dumbfounded. In the scrap of newspaper lay ten-rouble notes.
“My dear fellow, you really are unwell,” said Woland, shrugging his shoulders.
The barman, smiling wildly, got up from the stool.
“And,” he stammered, “and if they go and... again...”
“Hm...” the artiste pondered. “Well, then come and see us again. You are most welcome! Delighted to have made your acquaintance.”

Here Koroviev leaped out of the study, seized the barman’s hand, began shaking it and begging Andrei Fokich to give his regards to everyone, everyone. Barely understanding anything, the barman set off for the front hall.
“Hella, see him out!” Koroviev was shouting.

That naked redhead in the front hall again! The barman squeezed through the door, squeaked “Good-bye” and walked off like a drunk. After going a little way down, he stopped, sat on the steps, took out the package and checked: the ten-rouble notes were in place. Just then a woman with a green bag came out of the apartment that opened onto this landing. Seeing a man sitting on the step and staring dully at ten-rouble notes, she smiled and said pensively:

“What a building we’ve got... And this one’s drunk since morning. They’ve broken the window on the stairs again!” Looking more closely at the barman, she added: “Well, citizen, you’ve got tens to burn! How about sharing with me, eh?”
“Leave me be, for Christ’s sake,” said the barman in fright, and nimbly hid the money. The woman burst out laughing:
“Oh, go to the goblins, you skinflint! I was joking...” And she went on down.

The barman slowly got up, raised his hand to straighten his hat, and found that it was not on his head. He terribly did not want to go back, but he was sorry about the hat. After hesitating a little, he went back all the same and rang.
“What else do you want?” the accursed Hella asked him.

“I forgot my hat,” the barman whispered, poking at his bald head. Hella turned around; the barman spat mentally and shut his eyes. When he opened them, Hella was handing him his hat and a sword with a dark hilt.
“Not mine,” the barman whispered, pushing the sword away and quickly putting on the hat.
“Did you come without a sword, then?” Hella was surprised.

The barman grunted something and quickly went downstairs. For some reason his head felt uncomfortable and too warm in the hat; he took it off and, jumping with fright, gave a quiet cry. In his hands was a velvet beret with a bedraggled cock’s feather. The barman crossed himself. At that same instant the beret mewed, turned into a black kitten and, leaping back onto Andrei Fokich’s head, dug all its claws into his bald patch. Letting out a cry of despair, the barman rushed off downstairs, and the kitten fell off his head and shot off up the stairs.
Bursting out into the air, the barman trotted to the gates and left the devil’s building No. 302-bis forever.

What happened to him next is perfectly well known. Bursting out of the gateway, the barman glanced around rather wildly, as if looking for something. A minute later he was in the pharmacy across the street. No sooner had he uttered the words “Tell me, please...” than the woman behind the counter exclaimed:
“Citizen! Your whole head is cut to pieces!..”

Some five minutes later the barman had been bandaged with gauze, had learned that the best specialists in diseases of the liver were considered to be Professors Bernadsky and Kuzmin, had asked which was nearer, had lit up with joy on learning that Kuzmin lived literally across the courtyard in a little white mansion, and some two minutes later he was in this little mansion.

The premises were old-fashioned, but very, very cozy. The barman remembered that the first to meet him was a little old nanny who wanted to take his hat, but as he turned out to have no hat, the nanny, chewing with her toothless mouth, went off somewhere.

In her place there turned up by the mirror and, it seemed, under some sort of arch, a middle-aged woman, who at once said that an appointment could be made only for the nineteenth, no earlier. The barman at once grasped where salvation lay. Peering with a fading eye beyond the arch, where in what was plainly a waiting room three people sat waiting, he whispered:
“Mortally ill...”
The woman looked in perplexity at the barman’s bandaged head, hesitated, and said:
“Well, then...” and let the barman through beyond the arch.
At that same instant the opposite door opened, a gold pince-nez flashed in it, and a woman in a white coat said:
“Citizens, this patient will go out of turn.”
And before the barman could look around, he found himself in Professor Kuzmin’s consulting room. There was nothing frightening, solemn or medical about this long room.
“What’s the matter with you?” Professor Kuzmin asked in a pleasant voice, and glanced somewhat anxiously at the bandaged head.

“I have just learned from a reliable source,” the barman replied, glancing wildly at some group photograph under glass, “that in February of next year I am going to die of liver cancer. I beg you to stop it.”
Professor Kuzmin, just as he was sitting, leaned back against the tall Gothic leather back of his chair.
“Forgive me, I don’t understand you... have you been to a doctor, then? Why is your head bandaged?”

“Doctor? What doctor?.. You should have seen this doctor!..” the barman replied, and suddenly his teeth began to chatter. “And pay no attention to my head, it has nothing to do with it. Never mind the head, it’s got nothing to do with anything. Liver cancer, I beg you to stop it.”
“But, excuse me, who told you?”
“Believe him!” the barman pleaded fervently. “He knows, all right!”

“I don’t understand a thing,” the professor was saying, shrugging his shoulders and rolling his chair back from the desk. “How can he know when you are going to die? Especially since he is not a doctor!”
“In ward four,” replied the barman.
Here the professor looked at his patient, at his head, at his damp trousers, and thought: “That’s all I needed! A madman!” He asked:
“Do you drink vodka?”
“Never touched it,” replied the barman.

A minute later he had been undressed, was lying on a cold oilcloth couch, and the professor was kneading his belly. Here, it must be said, the barman cheered up considerably. The professor stated categorically that now, at least at the present moment, there were no signs of cancer in the barman. But that since this was so... since he was afraid and some charlatan had frightened him, all the tests ought to be done...

The professor scribbled on slips of paper, explaining where to go and what to take there. In addition he gave him a note to the professor of neuropathology Bure, explaining to the barman that his nerves were in a complete mess.
“How much do I owe you, professor?” the barman asked in a tender, trembling voice, pulling out a fat wallet.
“Whatever you like,” the professor answered curtly and drily.

The barman took out thirty roubles and laid them on the desk, and then, unexpectedly softly, as if operating with a cat’s paw, placed on top of the ten-rouble notes a little column wrapped in newspaper, which clinked.
“And what is this?” asked Kuzmin, and twirled his mustache.
“Don’t scorn it, citizen professor,” whispered the barman, “I beg you—stop the cancer.”

“Take your gold away at once,” said the professor, proud of himself. “You would do better to look after your nerves. Give a urine sample for analysis tomorrow, don’t drink a lot of tea, and eat without any salt at all.”
“Not even salt in the soup?” asked the barman.
“No salt in anything,” Kuzmin ordered.
“Ekhh!..” the barman exclaimed miserably, gazing at the professor with tender emotion, gathering up his gold pieces and backing toward the door.

The professor did not have many patients that evening, and as dusk approached the last one left. Taking off his white coat, the professor glanced at the spot where the barman had left the ten-rouble notes and saw that there were no ten-rouble notes there at all, but three labels from bottles of Abrau-Durso.

“The devil knows what this is!” muttered Kuzmin, trailing the skirt of his white coat on the floor and feeling the bits of paper. “It turns out he’s not only a schizophrenic but a crook as well! But I can’t understand what he wanted from me. Could it have been the note for the urine test? Oh! He’s stolen a coat!” And the professor rushed into the front hall, again with his white coat on one sleeve. “Ksenia Nikitishna!” he shouted shrilly in the doorway of the front hall. “Look and see, are the coats all there?”

It turned out that all the coats were there. But when the professor returned to his desk, having at last torn off his white coat, he seemed to grow into the parquet by the desk, his gaze riveted on its top. On the spot where the labels had lain sat an orphaned black kitten with an unhappy little face, mewing over a saucer of milk.
“Wh-what is this, if you please?! This is really...” Kuzmin felt the back of his head go cold.

At the professor’s quiet and plaintive cry Ksenia Nikitishna came running and calmed him down completely, telling him at once that some patient had of course abandoned the kitten there, and that this was a common thing with professors.
“They must live poorly,” Ksenia Nikitishna explained, “and here, of course, with us...”
They began to think and to guess who might have left it. Suspicion fell on a little old woman with a stomach ulcer.
“It’s her, of course,” Ksenia Nikitishna was saying. “This is how she thinks: I’m going to die anyway, but I’m sorry for the little kitten.”
“But excuse me!” shouted Kuzmin. “What about the milk?! Did she bring that too? And the saucer, eh?”
“She brought it in a little bottle and poured it into a saucer here,” Ksenia Nikitishna explained.
“In any case, take away both the kitten and the saucer,” said Kuzmin, and himself accompanied Ksenia Nikitishna to the door. When he came back, the situation had changed.

Hanging his white coat on its nail, the professor heard guffawing in the courtyard, looked out and, naturally, was dumbfounded. A lady in nothing but her slip was running across the courtyard to the little wing opposite. The professor even knew her name—Marya Alexandrovna. A boy was guffawing.
“What is this?” Kuzmin said contemptuously.

Here, on the other side of the wall, in the professor’s daughter’s room, a gramophone began to play the foxtrot “Hallelujah,” and at the same instant a sparrow’s chirping was heard behind the professor’s back. He turned around and saw a big sparrow hopping on his desk.

“Hm... keep calm...” thought the professor. “It flew in when I moved away from the window. Everything is in order!” the professor commanded himself, feeling that everything was in complete disorder and, of course, mainly because of this sparrow. Taking a closer look at it, the professor was at once convinced that this sparrow was not quite an ordinary sparrow. The nasty little sparrow was favoring its left foot, clearly clowning as it dragged it, working in syncopations—in a word, dancing the foxtrot to the sounds of the gramophone, like a drunk at a bar. It was being as insolent as it knew how, eyeing the professor brazenly.
Kuzmin’s hand came to rest on the telephone, and he was about to call his old classmate Bure to ask what sparrows of this sort meant at sixty, especially when one’s head suddenly began to spin.

Meanwhile the little sparrow settled on the inkstand he had been given as a present, fouled it (I am not joking!), then flew up, hung in the air, then, with a swing, as if with a steel beak, pecked at the glass of the photograph showing the entire university graduating class of ’94, smashed the glass to smithereens and only then flew out of the window.

The professor changed the number on the telephone and, instead of calling Bure, called the leech bureau, said that this was Professor Kuzmin speaking and that he requested that leeches be sent to his home at once.

Putting the receiver back on the hook, the professor again turned to his desk and at once let out a howl. At this desk sat a woman in a nurse’s headscarf with a handbag on which was written: “Leeches.” The professor howled when he peered into her mouth. It was a man’s mouth, crooked, stretching to the ears, with a single fang. The nurse’s eyes were dead.
“I’ll just tidy away the cash,” the nurse said in a man’s bass voice. “No sense in it lying about here.” She raked up the labels with a bird’s claw and began to melt into the air.

About two hours went by. Professor Kuzmin was sitting on his bed in his bedroom, with leeches hanging from his temples, behind his ears and on his neck. At Kuzmin’s feet, on the quilted silk eiderdown, sat gray-mustached Professor Bure, looking at Kuzmin with sympathy and consoling him that all this was nonsense. Outside the window it was already night.

What other strange things happened in Moscow that night we do not know and, of course, shall not try to find out—especially since the time is coming for us to pass on to the second part of this truthful narrative. Follow me, reader!
